solution_overview:
We are given the counts of health-club members attending Yoga ($Y$), Spin ($S$), and Pilates ($P$) out of a total of $N = 3000$ members. We model selecting a member uniformly at random, so probabilities are ratios of counts to $N$. We define the event counts and their corresponding probabilities:

Single event counts:
*   $|Y| = 1800 \implies P(Y) = \frac{1800}{3000} = 0.60$
*   $|S| = 1500 \implies P(S) = \frac{1500}{3000} = 0.50$
*   $|P| = 1200 \implies P(P) = \frac{1200}{3000} = 0.40$

Pairwise intersection counts:
*   $|Y \cap S| = 750 \implies P(Y \cap S) = \frac{750}{3000} = 0.25$
*   $|Y \cap P| = 600 \implies P(Y \cap P) = \frac{600}{3000} = 0.20$
*   $|S \cap P| = 450 \implies P(S \cap P) = \frac{450}{3000} = 0.15$

Triple intersection count:
*   $|Y \cap S \cap P| = 300 \implies P(Y \cap S \cap P) = \frac{300}{3000} = 0.10$

These probabilities are used with the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion for three sets. Let $S_1 = P(Y) + P(S) + P(P)$, $S_2 = P(Y \cap S) + P(Y \cap P) + P(S \cap P)$, and $S_3 = P(Y \cap S \cap P)$.

We calculate these sums:
$$S_1 = 0.60 + 0.50 + 0.40 = 1.50$$
$$S_2 = 0.25 + 0.20 + 0.15 = 0.60$$
$$S_3 = 0.10$$
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The probability that a member has at least one of the listed categories is given by the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion for three sets:
$$P(Y \cup S \cup P) = S_1 - S_2 + S_3$$
Using the pre-calculated sums:
$$P(Y \cup S \cup P) = 1.50 - 0.60 + 0.10$$
$$P(Y \cup S \cup P) = 0.90 + 0.10$$
$$P(Y \cup S \cup P) = 1.00$$
The probability of attending at least one category is $1.00$, or $100\%$. Since $100\% \ge 95\%$, the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The probability that a member attended exactly one of the listed categories can be calculated using the inclusion-exclusion formula for exactly one event:
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = S_1 - 2S_2 + 3S_3$$
Using the pre-calculated sums:
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 1.50 - 2(0.60) + 3(0.10)$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 1.50 - 1.20 + 0.30$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.30 + 0.30$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.60$$
The probability of attending exactly one category is $0.60$, or $60\%$. Since $60\% > 55\%$, the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The probability that a member attended exactly two of the listed categories can be calculated using the inclusion-exclusion formula for exactly two events:
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = S_2 - 3S_3$$
Using the pre-calculated sums:
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.60 - 3(0.10)$$
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.60 - 0.30$$
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.30$$
The probability of attending exactly two categories is $0.30$, or $30\%$. Since $30\% \ge 25\%$, the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The probability that a member attended none of the listed categories is the complement of attending at least one category:
$$P(\text{none}) = 1 - P(Y \cup S \cup P)$$
From part A, $P(Y \cup S \cup P) = 1.00$. Substituting this value:
$$P(\text{none}) = 1 - 1.00$$
$$P(\text{none}) = 0.00$$
The probability of attending none of the categories is $0.00$, or $0\%$. Since the claim states $0\%$, the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The probability of attending "at least two" categories means attending exactly two categories or attending all three categories. This is the sum of the probability of exactly two and the probability of all three:
$$P(\text{at least two}) = P(\text{exactly two}) + P(Y \cap S \cap P)$$
From part C, $P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.30$. The probability of all three is $P(Y \cap S \cap P) = S_3 = 0.10$.
$$P(\text{at least two}) = 0.30 + 0.10$$
$$P(\text{at least two}) = 0.40$$
The claim compares this to "double all three". This value is $2 \times P(Y \cap S \cap P)$:
$$2 \times P(Y \cap S \cap P) = 2 \times 0.10$$
$$2 \times P(Y \cap S \cap P) = 0.20$$
Comparing the two values, $0.40$ (for at least two) and $0.20$ (for double all three), we find $0.40 > 0.20$, so the statement is True.
